article.title: Why Too Many Choices Can Make Us Less Satisfied
article.framework: More Options → Higher Comparison Cost → More Foregone Alternatives → Regret → Lower Satisfaction
article.coreIdea: More choice increases opportunity as well as comparison costs: once alternatives become numerous and visible, people may gain freedom while also becoming more aware of everything they did not choose.
article.body:
Imagine opening a streaming service on Friday night. You have hundreds of films available, recommendations tailored to your taste, and almost no cost for switching from one title to another. This sounds like an ideal form of consumer freedom. Yet twenty minutes later, you may still be scrolling. Eventually you choose something, but halfway through the film you wonder whether another option would have been better. More choice has given you more possibilities, but not necessarily more satisfaction.

This tension is often described as choice overload. The basic idea is not that choice is bad. Having alternatives can protect people from poor products, allow different preferences to be served, and give individuals a sense of control. The problem appears when the number or complexity of options makes comparison costly. Choosing between three restaurants is one task; comparing eighty restaurants by price, distance, rating, cuisine, waiting time, and atmosphere is a different one.

Every additional option can provide potential value, but it also adds information to process. This creates cognitive load. Human attention and working memory are limited, so people cannot compare every feature of every alternative with equal care. They simplify. They filter by ratings, choose familiar brands, copy friends, or stop searching once an option seems good enough. These shortcuts are not necessarily irrational. They are responses to scarcity—specifically, scarcity of attention and decision time.

Choice also creates opportunity cost. In economics, the opportunity cost of a decision is the value of the best alternative you give up. If you spend Saturday afternoon at a concert, you cannot use the same hours for a museum visit. With only one realistic alternative, the sacrifice may be easy to ignore. But when ten attractive alternatives are visible, the things you are giving up become psychologically harder to forget.

This helps explain why satisfaction can fall even when the chosen option itself is excellent. Suppose you order pasta from a menu with four dishes and enjoy it. Now imagine ordering the same pasta from a menu with forty dishes, including several meals you also like. The pasta has not changed. What has changed is the comparison set. Your mind can generate more counterfactuals: perhaps the steak would have been better, perhaps the seafood was more special, perhaps you should have tried something new.

Counterfactual thinking means imagining how reality could have been different. It is useful because it helps us learn from mistakes. However, after a decision, it can also feed regret. The more attractive the rejected alternatives are, the easier it becomes to construct a better imaginary outcome. Satisfaction is therefore influenced not only by what we receive but also by what we can imagine having received instead.

This connects to reference points. In earlier lessons, we saw that people evaluate outcomes relative to a benchmark rather than in isolation. A large choice set can create multiple possible benchmarks at once. Your actual choice competes not with one clear alternative but with an ideal combination of features taken from many alternatives. A phone may have the best camera but not the longest battery life. Another may be cheaper but less attractive. The chosen phone can then be compared with an imaginary device that has every competitor's strongest feature.

Online platforms can intensify this effect because they make alternatives unusually visible. Before digital marketplaces, a shopper might compare products in two or three nearby stores. Today, search engines and platforms can display hundreds of options, reviews, rankings, and prices within seconds. Search friction has fallen dramatically. But reducing search friction can increase comparison friction: finding alternatives becomes easier while deciding among them becomes harder.

This is a useful reminder that friction is not a single thing. Removing one obstacle can move the difficulty elsewhere. A dating app may make meeting new people easier but make commitment harder if users remain aware of many possible alternatives. A job platform may make vacancies easier to discover while increasing anxiety about whether a better opportunity is still available. Technology can reduce the friction of access without reducing the friction of evaluation.

Not everyone reacts to large choice sets in the same way. Psychologists sometimes distinguish between maximizing and satisficing. A maximizer tries to identify the best possible option, while a satisficer looks for an option that meets an acceptable standard. Maximizing can be useful when the decision is important and comparison is manageable. But when options are numerous, the search for the absolute best can become expensive because each additional possibility seems to deserve evaluation.

A satisficing rule reduces the search space. Instead of asking, “Which laptop is objectively best?”, someone might ask, “Which laptop meets my requirements for battery life, weight, and price?” Once an option passes those thresholds, the search can stop. This does not guarantee the theoretical optimum, but it lowers decision costs. In many ordinary decisions, the value of finding a slightly better option may be smaller than the time and attention required to find it.

This introduces an important concept: the value of information. More information is useful only when it can improve the decision enough to justify the cost of obtaining and processing it. Reading one more review may reveal a serious product defect. Reading the fiftieth review may simply repeat what you already know while exposing you to another minor complaint. At some point, additional information has diminishing returns.

Measurement matters here too. If a platform measures success only by the number of available products, it may conclude that more is always better. But quantity is a poor proxy for decision quality. Better metrics might include purchase completion, return rates, time spent searching, post-purchase satisfaction, or whether customers come back. As with Goodhart's Law, optimizing an easy metric can move the system away from the broader objective.

That feedback loop matters. Popular items receive more clicks, which generate more reviews and data, which can improve their ranking, which creates still more visibility. The original abundance remains in theory, but attention becomes concentrated in practice. So the important resource is no longer merely the number of available options. It is the scarce attention through which those options must pass.

The broader lesson is not that we should always choose less. Some decisions deserve extensive comparison, especially when errors are costly or difficult to reverse. The lesson is to distinguish the value of another option from the cost of evaluating it. More possibilities improve a decision only when we can use them productively.

A practical question is therefore: “What information could realistically change my decision?” If another hour of searching is unlikely to change the answer, continuing may create more counterfactuals than value. Setting criteria in advance can also prevent the target from moving every time a new option appears.

Choice is valuable because it gives us alternatives. But alternatives have a psychological cost once we must compare them, reject them, and live with the knowledge that they existed. The goal is not to find a world with no missed opportunities. It is to make decisions in which the opportunities we give up do not become more important than the one we actually chose.
article.summaryZh:
今天把一个看似简单的命题拆开：more choice 为什么不一定带来 more satisfaction？关键是选择同时产生两种东西——option value 和 comparison cost。更多选项扩大了可能性，但也增加信息处理、机会成本和反事实想象。

第一条机制是 attention scarcity。选项从 3 个增加到 80 个以后，我们并没有同步获得更多工作记忆和决策时间，于是会使用 rating、品牌、朋友意见、默认推荐等 shortcut。这可以接回 friction：数字平台降低了 search friction，却可能提高 comparison friction。一个摩擦被消除，并不代表系统总摩擦一定下降，它可能只是换了位置。

第二条机制是 opportunity cost → counterfactual → regret。被放弃的优质选项越可见，我们越容易想象“另一个可能更好”。于是 satisfaction 不再只取决于 chosen outcome，还取决于 comparison set。大量选择甚至会制造一个现实中不存在的“完美参照物”：把 A 的相机、B 的续航、C 的价格拼成 imaginary benchmark，再拿真实产品与它比较。

第三条是 maximizing vs satisficing。面对巨大 choice set，寻找绝对最优解的边际收益可能越来越低，而信息处理成本继续增加。今天因此加入一个新工具：Value of Information。继续搜索之前问：下一条信息有多大概率真正改变决定？如果不能改变决定，更多信息可能只是在制造更多 counterfactuals。

它还能连接 measurement 和 feedback：平台若把“选择数量”当成功指标，可能忽视 decision quality；而选择越多，用户越依赖 rankings 和 algorithms，注意力反而可能集中到少数热门选项。今天的核心不是“少选项更好”，而是：More options are valuable only when the value of additional information exceeds the cost of evaluating it。

speaking.question: Do you think having more choices always makes consumers happier?
speaking.framework: Freedom → Comparison cost → Opportunity cost → Satisfaction
speaking.response: No, I don't think more choice always leads to greater satisfaction. Having several alternatives is useful because people have different needs, but after a certain point the comparison itself becomes costly. If I have to evaluate dozens of similar products, I may spend a lot of time worrying about small differences. More importantly, a large choice set makes the options I reject more visible, so even after making a good decision I can imagine that another one might have been better. I think choice is most helpful when people have enough alternatives to match their preferences but also have a clear way to narrow them down.
expressions: More choice does not always lead to greater satisfaction.
After a certain point, the comparison itself becomes costly.
Choice is most helpful when people have a clear way to narrow the options down.

speaking.question: How has technology changed the way people make decisions?
speaking.framework: Lower search friction → More information → Higher evaluation cost → Greater reliance on filters
speaking.response: Technology has made it much easier to discover alternatives, which is generally a good thing, but it has also changed where the difficulty lies. In the past, people might struggle to find enough information, whereas today the problem is often deciding what deserves attention. We can compare hundreds of hotels, jobs or products in minutes, but processing all that information is impossible. As a result, people rely more on ratings, rankings, algorithms and recommendations. So technology has reduced the friction of finding options, but in many cases it has increased the importance of filtering them well.
expressions: Technology has changed where the difficulty lies.
The problem is often deciding what deserves attention.
Technology has reduced the friction of finding options.

expressions.expression: After a certain point, the comparison itself becomes costly.
